paths.title: Infrastructure as Code
paths.description: Manage cloud resources through reviewed, repeatable, state-aware definitions.
concept: Infrastructure as code makes environments reviewable and repeatable, but errors can affect entire systems.
Modules, state, secrets, permissions, and plans require the same discipline as application code.
workflow: Review the intended plan before changing live resources.
Small, reversible changes reduce drift and unexpected replacement.
Generate a plan against the correct environment.
Review creates, updates, replacements, and deletions.
Verify resource health and record the result.
question: Prevent configuration drift
What most directly reduces differences between documented and actual infrastructure?
Manual console changes without records
Applying reviewed infrastructure code through one controlled workflow
Renaming screenshots
Ignoring state
A controlled infrastructure-as-code path makes desired state explicit and reduces untracked changes.
checklist: Confirm that the plan is scoped, reversible, and observable.
The most dangerous change may be an implicit resource replacement.
The target account and region are verified.
The plan contains no unexpected deletion.
Secrets stay outside source control and logs.
Rollback or forward-fix steps are known.

paths.title: CI/CD and Release Safety
paths.description: Build immutable artifacts, enforce quality gates, and deploy progressively with rollback.
concept: Build once, promote the same artifact
Rebuilding separately for each environment can create differences that were never tested.
An immutable artifact should move through verification and environments while configuration is injected separately.
workflow: Make every release traceable from source to deployed artifact.
Automation should stop on failed checks and apply stronger controls to higher-risk changes.
Pin the source commit and dependencies.
Run syntax, unit, integration, and security checks.
Verify metrics and retain rollback capability.
question: Use progressive delivery
Why release to a small cohort before full traffic?
To avoid all testing
To limit impact while observing real behavior
To remove monitoring
To guarantee no defect exists
A canary or staged rollout bounds the blast radius and provides production evidence before wider exposure.
checklist: Confirm that the deployment can be trusted and reversed.
A successful pipeline run should identify exactly what was deployed and where.
Required checks passed on the deployed commit.
The artifact is immutable and identifiable.

paths.title: Reliability and Observability
paths.description: Define service objectives, monitor user impact, and design bounded failure behavior.
concept: Reliability is measured from the user boundary
Service-level indicators quantify outcomes such as successful requests, latency, freshness, or job completion.
Resource metrics are diagnostic signals, but they do not replace measures of user success.
workflow: Choose a measure that drives engineering and operational decisions.
An objective should define both the event being measured and the population of events.
Set an objective based on business need.
Link alerts to diagnosis and response guidance.
question: Choose a useful alert
Which alert is closest to user impact?
One server reached 60% CPU briefly
Checkout success rate dropped below its objective
A log file grew by one line
A dashboard color changed
Checkout success directly measures a critical user outcome and can be compared with a defined objective.
checklist: Verify that common failures degrade safely and can be diagnosed.
Resilience includes limits that prevent one dependency from exhausting the whole system.
Timeouts are shorter than caller deadlines.
Retries are bounded with backoff and jitter.
